prime.problem: An O(n) Python loop over numbers can still be hundreds of times slower than it needs to be: adding 17 to 10⁷ ints took 0.582 s as a loop and 0.00286 s with NumPy on the M3. The algorithm is fine; the cost is per-item bookkeeping.
prime.fits: Sixth estimation card. Algorithm-beats-hardware said the constant c matters once f(n) is optimal, and the compilers card said CPython won't shrink c for you. This card opens one loop iteration to see where c goes, and changes the engine instead.
expect: boxed objects vs raw machine values
prime.goal: Explain where a Python loop's time goes per item, predict when NumPy will help and when it won't, and pick the right alternative for a loop that can't be vectorized.

attend: Of the source's five per-item steps inside INPLACE_ADD, which is the only one NumPy also does?
Why does a list of ints cost 36 B per item while an int64 array costs 8?
Why does np.abs(a).mean() peak at 80 MB of extra memory, and how does chunking cap it?
Which three meanings does "vectorization" have, and which one is the card's main point?
What kinds of loop have no array form, and what does the card suggest for them?

must: A list holds pointers to full int objects → each l[i] += 17 dispatches ~11 bytecodes, checks types, calls a C function and allocates a new 28-byte int → the add itself is a tiny fraction of 58.2 ns per item
A NumPy array holds raw 8-byte ints → a += 17 is one C loop of load, add, store (plus SIMD) → 0.286 ns per item, 203× faster, with the same O(n)
Each vectorized step materialises a full-size temporary → np.abs(a).mean() allocates another 80 MB at 10⁷ items → chunking (10⁵ at a time) caps the peak at ~800 KB

Vectorization needs the same operation on many items of one type → branches or recurrences like x[i] = f(x[i-1]) have no array form → compile the loop instead (Numba, PyPy for pure Python), and check the algorithm first
elevated: The same data costs 36 B per item as a list of ints (8 B pointer + 28 B object) vs 8 B in an int64 array → 360 MB vs 80 MB at 10⁷ → memory traffic, not only instructions, is part of the 203×
reference: the source's PyPy and Numba timings

compress.prompt: From memory, draw one iteration of l[i] += 17 as a strip: which steps are bookkeeping and which one is the add. Next to it, draw NumPy's inner loop. Then write two sentences on when vectorizing fails.
checklist: Python: dispatch bytecodes, look up the type's add, unbox both, add, box a new int, store the pointer
NumPy: load 8 bytes, add, store 8 bytes (several per SIMD instruction)
58.2 ns vs 0.286 ns per item on the M3
fails on memory (temporaries), branches and recurrences, and tiny inputs
Numba or PyPy compile the loop itself

retrieve.q: Explain why vectorizing doesn't change the complexity yet can be 200× faster.
answer: both versions touch each item once: O(n)
vectorizing removes the per-item interpreter bookkeeping and object allocation
it only cuts the constant, from 58.2 to 0.286 ns per item

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens inside the single bytecode INPLACE_ADD for the list at index 1000.
answer: look up the type of the int object and its add slot
call that C function with both objects
read the machine integers out of both
allocate a new 28-byte int to hold the result

retrieve.q: Your per-item logic has an if/else and each item depends on the previous one. NumPy, Numba or PyPy: which does the card point you to, and what does each cost?
answer: NumPy can't express the dependency without a loop
Numba compiles your own loop and works with NumPy arrays: a dependency and a first compile
PyPy JITs pure-Python loops but interfaces poorly with NumPy
a C/Cython/Rust extension works but adds a build step

compare.q: The compilers card fixed the string loop by changing the algorithm; this card fixes the add loop by changing the engine. Why was each the right fix for its loop?
answer: the string loop was O(n²): no engine fixes growth
the add loop is already O(n): only the constant can improve

compare.q: cs-6 says an in-memory database's remaining cost is the CPU waiting on cache misses. How does NumPy's contiguous array help with the same problem that a list of pointers makes worse?
answer: a list scatters int objects across the heap: each item is a pointer chase
an array stores values back to back, so each cache line holds 8 int64s
the layout decides how many cache misses happen, in both cards

predict.q: Your data starts as a Python list of 10⁷ ints. You write np.array(l) + 17 once and convert back with .tolist(). Before trying: do you get anything like the 203× speed-up over the plain loop? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: No, not for a single operation. np.array(l) has to visit all 10⁷ Python int objects to unbox them, and .tolist() allocates 10⁷ new ones: the same kind of per-item work the loop did. The 203× applies to work done while data stays in the array. Convert once, do many operations, convert back once (or never).

apply.task: On your machine, time four versions of "add 17 to every item" for 10⁶ items: the card's index loop, a list comprehension, map with a lambda, and NumPy a += 17. Report nanoseconds per item for each. Then compute the memory per item for a list of floats vs a float64 array, using sys.getsizeof.
apply.done: You have four ns-per-item figures, ranked, with NumPy far ahead and the three pure-Python versions within a small factor of each other; and your memory line reads 8 B pointer + 24 B float object = 32 B per item vs 8 B in the array (32 MB vs 8 MB for 10⁶).
apply.hint: timeit.timeit(stmt, number=1) on a fresh list each time; sys.getsizeof(1.0) is 24 in CPython 3.10.
